The Price of Greed

🔹A fox happened to fall into a well bucket and, as the rope turned, went down to the bottom of the well. Struggle as it might, it found no way out—until a hungry wolf came to the well's edge and lowered its head.

🔹The clever fox put on an act and cried out: "Down here a feast of food and comfort awaits, but I can't manage it alone; if you'd like to share the meal, get into the upper bucket so you can come down to me!"

🔹The greedy wolf leapt without a moment's hesitation and sat in the upper bucket. Since the wolf was heavier, its bucket hurtled downward, and at the same time the rope turned and drew the fox's bucket upward.

🔹Midway up the well, the two buckets passed each other. The wolf cried out in astonishment: "Where are you off to, friend?!"

🔹The fox laughed and said: "That's the way of this wheel of fortune—unless one goes down, the other never comes up!" The fox reached the bright mouth of the well and sprang out, while the wolf was left behind in the dark depths.

🔹A group of citizens in Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, gathered on Monday outside the Republic of Azerbaijan Embassy; participants held placards with slogans including "The hijab is not an obstacle to knowledge," "The hijab is a right, not a privilege," and "Silence in the face of injustice is a crime."

Ankara; Protest Outside the Republic of Azerbaijan Embassy

🔹Last Tuesday, protesters gathered outside the Republic of Azerbaijan Embassy in Ankara, the capital of Turkey. The event was held at the invitation of Turkey's Hizb ut-Tahrir party, and Abdullah Imamoglu, a writer and religious activist, read the gathering's statement.

Istanbul; Security Measures Outside the Consulate

🔹Simultaneously with the Ankara gathering, a group of protesters also gathered outside the Republic of Azerbaijan Consulate General in Istanbul; police established extensive security measures around the consulate and police vehicles blocked the entrance to the building.

Domestic car prices are peaking ahead of the dollar🔹Car prices in the market have become sticky to the currency—a trend that accelerates upward whenever the exchange rate climbs. Today, cars that were once considered economy models have crossed into the billions of tomans.🔹This dependence on the currency, especially over the past year, has opened a deep gap between people's purchasing power and real prices. Last autumn, around this same time, the market was at completely different price levels, but persistent currency instability released the spring of prices.🔹Market statistics from the past year lay bare the depth of this jump: the Dena Automatic, which was around 1 billion and 300 million tomans at this point last year, has now reached about 4 billion tomans, and in the assembled-products segment, Lamari has climbed from 2 billion and 500 million tomans last year to 7 billion and 400 million tomans.🔹The car market's dependence on dollar fluctuations stands in clear contradiction to the claim of self-sufficiency. While Iran Khodro cites 78 percent localization and Saipa 81 percent, and assemblers hold a share of less than 40 percent, the question arises: why has localization failed to shield prices from currency shocks?🔸To curb this cycle and sever the car market's psychological and real dependence on the dollar, policymakers have no choice but to open the doors to targeted imports at times when relative stability prevails in the country's management of currency resources, so that part of the currency is channeled into bringing in economy cars—a strategy that can break the monopoly and rescue the market from profiteering.@Farsna - Link
